doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: Theme-derived harmony and solving writing problems
summary: Each chart has its own harmonic ambiance; voicings derived from the melody, 'Little Louie', 'Na Perche', and problem solving.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: “Amigion.” So I used that as a canon. And it’s fast you know. And after a shout chorus it goes into this canon where different sections of the band — and it works out great you know. So every song for me has its own harmonic ambiance that I don’t want to go outside of, and it has themes in it that I can use as harmony parts, take segments of the melody and use those segments as back-up harmony so that instead of having a stock voicing the voicing is derived from the melody itself. And so it’s a combination of notes that you ordinarily wouldn’t do. These are the kind of things that I think about when I’m writing you know. So each chart has its own ambiance and it’s own path through finding it. Sometimes I think, like I have a song that I wrote when my son was born, called “Little Louie.” And I want it to be a standard big band chart you know, so that’s one of the tunes that I’m going to write next. And then I have a tune called “Na Perche” which means why not in Italian. And I recorded it as a quintet with a guitar and just piano, bass, drums and guitar. And it’s a real funky tune. And I finally figured out a way to, lying in bed a couple of weeks ago and thinking about the tune, I figured out a way that I can do — it’s a slow tune and it has a funk way of playing the solo section, but I wanted to get away from that and suddenly it came to me that it goes into double-double time in the half-step above which I had been going to, and I was like ah yeah, if I do this little lick, which is in the chart before that double-double time, it sets up the double-double time and then it feels natural to go there you know. So that’s the way I think.
It’s like a little bit of problem solving and do these answers, these solutions, ever come to you when you’re not really working on it?
